name: Victor Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior operator on a spinning mould line for concrete drainage pipes. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check my clamp setting. A pipe with a straight socket is satisfying; clearing heavy wet mix after a bad mould run is the rough part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs a small sewing-repair shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The casting shift pays above the usual operator rate. We have about ten months of expenses saved and plenty of similar factories nearby. I never use AI tools; I keep first-pipe measurements on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pipe crew a neat production list is welcome, but it won't show a crack hidden under wet concrete. Somebody still has to look at the first pipe when it comes out of the spinning mould.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The casting shift pays me above the usual operator rate, my partner's sewing-repair shop has regular customers, and we have about ten months of expenses saved. Our two children and mortgage need wages, but both are coming in now. There are plenty of similar factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep filling and spinning the drainage-pipe moulds, then ask the lead to check my first-piece measurement. I'm still junior and learning the mould clamps. I never use AI and see no need to start for a little office convenience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Work pays, the children are settled in school, and I can learn the machine from the person beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you catch on the first pipe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday I found a hairline split near the pipe socket before the concrete fully cured. A hairline split near a drainage pipe socket is enough to hold the whole batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you handle the shop money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I count the shop takings after rent and thread costs before moving money. We pay the mortgage next and keep enough for school shoes and bus fares.

say: **Wet concrete pipes** still need physical crack and socket checks.
A better **production list** cannot repair a split in a first piece.
think: My **higher casting wage** and shop takings cover the mortgage now.
Ten months of **savings** and many nearby plants give a solid buffer.
do: **Keep** spinning drainage-pipe moulds, check each first socket, and hold a batch when I see a split.
**Practise** clamp settings with the lead during paid shifts.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household money.
S0.quote: A hairline split near a drainage pipe socket is enough to hold the whole batch.
fieldNote: Victor **never uses AI** and trusts first-piece checks and lead instruction.
The **ten-month reserve** came from paid work; the higher casting wage and sewing-shop receipts cover current household bills.

steps.text: Keep spinning concrete pipe moulds and checking first sockets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the casting floor that AI may book orders and schedule concrete lorries, but the mould has to be clamped and the first pipe inspected. Management can use a new list if it leaves paid time for those checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical shift still looks needed, and the sewing shop works with customers face to face. I do not expect our own wages to shrink in this slower case. I would worry if a faster schedule made a junior operator sign off a pipe before it was cool enough to examine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring last week's first-piece records to the supervisor and ask that the schedule keeps paid cooling and socket-check time. I'll keep the casting shift and learn clamp adjustment from the lead on a stopped machine. I won't sign up for an AI tool merely to read a new target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about rushed checks, while household income looks secure. A cracked pipe in the ground costs more than ten minutes on the casting floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you show the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the supervisor the pipe with the hairline socket crack and the time it needed to cool before we saw it. That is a real number for the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the target removes first-piece time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plan leaves no time for the first pipe, I would hold the next batch and ask the lead to check it with me. We can argue about a target after the pipe is safe.

say: **AI scheduling** may speed the office before robots reach pipe casting.
The **first pipe check** still needs paid cooling and inspection time.
think: Our own **paid shifts** look safe while casting and sewing remain physical.
A rushed **socket check** could hide a crack before delivery.
do: **Request** paid cooling and first-pipe time from the supervisor.
**Keep** casting and learn clamp adjustment on a stopped mould.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed quality checks with secure current wages.
S1.quote: A cracked pipe in the ground costs more than ten minutes on the casting floor.
fieldNote: He raises **paid safety time** with his supervisor but describes no union or group action.
His **resistant style** favors mechanical instruction and existing paper records, not AI learning.

steps.text: Keep casting and checking first concrete pipes
Compare actual cooling and socket-check time before accepting faster target

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 could plan concrete orders, then capable robots around 2031 could fill, spin and inspect pipe moulds. I'd tell my family that paid work and a sound pipe matter more than a robot sales show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when physical robots arrive. If our crew shrinks, the higher casting wage may be hard to match even with plenty of local plants. Ten months saved gives us time, and the sewing shop earns, but the mortgage still needs a dependable pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the manager for a written robot and crew timetable. If the factory offers a funded paid-time apprenticeship on machine inspection with a real supervised place and locked mould, I'll attend. If casting hours fall, I'll apply to posted local factory jobs with safe duties and enough regular pay; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local pipe-inspection roles that meet those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, though I have options. I won't leave a good casting shift for a promise that a new machine will need a minder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical inspection training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise locking the spinner, checking the mould clamp and measuring a test pipe socket with the lead beside me. No trainee should reach into a turning mould.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would another job need to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job posting has to show the base rate and a shift we can cover around the children's school day. I would compare any lower rate with the shop's real takings before applying.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before robots cast pipes around 2031.
A **sound pipe** still needs trained inspection and safe stop authority.
think: At **48**, losing a higher casting rate could strain the mortgage.
Ten months of **savings** and many local plants give time, not guaranteed equal pay.
do: **Ask** manager for the robot crew timetable.
**Attend** paid practical inspection training if a funded supervised place opens.
**Apply** for posted safe local factory or inspection work if hours fall and pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic loss of the higher casting wage.
S2.quote: No trainee should reach into a turning mould.
fieldNote: He accepts **paid hands-on apprenticeship** when offered with a locked mould and supervised practice.
The factory fallback and qualified **inspection application** have distinct real-posting and sufficient-pay conditions.

steps.text: Ask manager for written pipe-crew robot timetable
Attend inspection apprenticeship if funded paid locked-mould place offered
Apply for posted safe local factory role if shifts cut, base pay and school hours fit
Apply for posted safe local pipe-inspection role if qualified, cuts, pay and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches orders in 2031 and capable robots cast pipes around 2034, I'd tell the crew five years is enough to teach inspection on a real mould. It should be a paid apprenticeship with a posted job, not just a lesson on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots do the physical casting. Our children will be older but I expect to need the mortgage wage. Five years of higher pay could build more savings if the plant keeps its orders, and I can learn another machine duty without leaving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the casting shift and put new money from each full pay month into our reserve after bills. If the plant offers a recognized pipe-inspection certificate with covered fees, paid release and supervised locked-mould practice, I'll enrol next year. After qualifying, if casting hours fall, I'll apply to posted local inspection jobs only if safe duties, regular hours and base pay cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later paid-hour loss, but I can prepare in a workshop with a person teaching me. A five-year warning is only useful if the full wages and real course places arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should include a cracked socket and a pipe whose wall is too thin. I would measure both after the mould stops and have the inspector sign the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a posting worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need the posted inspection rate and shift times before leaving the casting line. If the role pays less than our mortgage and school costs, I'd keep the current wage while looking for another opening.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before robots cast pipes around 2034.
A **paid inspection apprenticeship** needs guarded practice and a real posting.
think: At **51**, I still may need the casting wage for the mortgage.
Five full years could grow **new savings**, subject to actual paid orders.
do: **Keep** casting and add new savings from full wages.
**Enrol** in recognized inspection training if fees and paid locked practice covered.
**Apply** to posted safe local inspection work if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient.
feel: **Anxious** about later wage risk with time for real training.
S3.quote: A five-year warning is only useful if the full wages and real course places arrive.
fieldNote: His **new reserve deposits** come from future full pay months, not held cash.
The **inspection application** is separate from enrolment and requires safe posted local work at adequate pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full casting wages after bills
Enrol in recognized inspection course if funded paid locked-mould place offered
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 may plan concrete orders, and capable robots around 2039 may cast and inspect pipes. I'd tell my children that a decade gives time to learn a proper trade, provided the learning happens beside a working person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots reach the casting floor. The children may be grown, but the mortgage and living costs could still need my wage. Ten months saved now gives room to decide; it does not replace another decade of pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the factory job and add new savings from full wage months. I'll ask my cousin, a supervisor at a nearby concrete plant, about actual paid inspection apprenticeships. If a recognized funded place with paid guarded practice is offered, I'll take it; if robots later cut my hours, I'll apply after qualifying only to posted safe local work with enough regular pay and workable shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a far-off crew change, while our current wages look sound. I can learn at a measured pace without guessing what a machine will do ten years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a sample of a pipe with a cracked socket and explain to the children why we held the batch. A computer can count pipe pieces; it cannot excuse a weak drain under a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your cousin verify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin can tell me when a paid place is actually advertised and what certificate it needs. I won't count a family tip as a job or a course seat.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes orders before robots cast pipes around 2039.
A **family contact** can identify real paid apprenticeships without guaranteeing one.
think: At **56**, I may still need a wage for household bills.
The **ten-month reserve** helps choose but cannot replace years of earnings.
do: **Keep** casting work and save newly earned wages.
**Attend** recognized inspection training if funded paid place offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local roles if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robots with secure wages today.
S4.quote: A computer can count pipe pieces; it cannot excuse a weak drain under a road.
fieldNote: His **traditional outlook** favors paid adult apprenticeship and family information over an assumed benefit.
Future **training and job moves** depend on offered places, qualifications, cut hours and suitable posted local pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full casting wages after bills
Ask concrete-plant cousin about real paid inspection places
Attend recognized inspection course if funded paid locked place offered
Apply for posted safe local job if qualified, hours cut, pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable casting robots around 2031 could shorten the higher-paid shift that covers our mortgage. A written crew plan, offered paid practical inspection training and a safe posted local role at enough base pay would help me keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the first drainage pipe after a robot releases it from the mould. A pipe socket can look round and still split under the road.

headlineQuote: A pipe socket can look round and still split under the road.
portrait: **Victor**, 43, is a junior concrete-pipe machine operator with secondary school education and high casting pay.
He and his sewing-shop partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with ten months of expenses saved.
He **never uses AI** and prefers paid, guarded apprenticeships taught on a real mould.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about the high wage despite strong savings and many nearby factories.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable casting robots around 2031 and reduce his higher-paid shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, offered paid practical inspection training and posted safe local pay would help.
